chapters.title: Chapter 2: Global Cycles That Shaped Modern Markets

lessons.title: Japan's Lost Decades: When a Cycle Refuses to Turn

body.text: "Just wait, it always comes back" is usually good advice, and Japan is the reason it cannot be a guarantee. The Nikkei took 34 years to regain its 1989 peak, because the engines underneath the cycle, credit, land, banks and population, stayed broken for a generation.

children.text: Every lesson so far has ended with some version of recovery. Even the Dow, after 1929, eventually got back. Japan is different, and not because it was a poor or badly run country. In 1989 it was the second largest economy in the world, admired for its manufacturing, its savings rate and its companies. It then went through a bust so long that economists named it by the decade: the lost decade, then the lost decades. For any investor who assumes a broad index must recover within a few years, this is the case study to keep in mind.

The displacement came from abroad. Under the Plaza Accord of September 1985, the major economies agreed to push the US dollar down. The yen roughly doubled in value against the dollar within about three years, from around 240 to around 125. To protect exporters from the stronger yen, the Bank of Japan cut interest rates to 2.5% by early 1987, a record low at the time, and kept them there. Cheap money flowed into the two assets Japanese banks liked best as collateral: land and shares. Companies borrowed to speculate in financial markets, a practice popular enough to get its own name, zaitech. When the government sold shares in the telecom company NTT in 1987, the stock roughly tripled within months of listing.

children.text: Japan's bubble is the credit loop from Lesson 1.3 running at national scale:
Land prices rise, so the land a company owns is worth more as collateral.
Banks lend the company more against that land.
The company uses the loans to buy more land and shares, including shares of the bank and of its business partners.
Land and share prices rise further, the company's assets look even stronger, and the loop repeats.

Because Japanese banks and companies owned large stakes in each other, known as cross-shareholdings, falling share prices later damaged bank capital and corporate balance sheets at the same time. The loop that built the bubble also guaranteed that the bust would hit everything together.

body.text: Two famous signs of the peak. By 1989 the Japanese stock market was, by value, larger than the US stock market, for an economy less than half the size. And a widely repeated estimate held that the land under the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was worth more than all the real estate in California. Whether or not that calculation was precise, the fact that people repeated it approvingly tells you where the cycle was.

children.text: The Turn, and the Rallies That Fooled Everyone

Worried about land prices and inflation, the Bank of Japan raised its discount rate from 2.5% in May 1989 to 6% by August 1990. In April 1990 the Ministry of Finance also told banks to limit the growth of their property lending. The credit loop reversed. The Nikkei lost almost 40% in 1990 alone. Land prices peaked a little later, around 1991, and then fell year after year; commercial land in the big cities eventually lost more than 80% of its peak value. What made the Japanese bust so damaging for investors was not just its depth. It was the series of convincing recoveries that turned out to be traps.

children.text: Each of those rallies was big enough to convince investors that the bottom was in. A 141% rise over four years is a genuine bull market by any definition. Yet an investor who bought at the 2007 high was below their purchase price two years later, and the index in March 2009 was about 82% below its 1989 peak, almost two decades on. Only after 2012 did a sustained recovery begin.

body.label: The longest wait among major markets
body.context: The Nikkei closed at 38,916 on 29 December 1989, and first closed above that level on 22 February 2024.

body.title: What Recovery Required
body.prompt: The Nikkei stood at about 7,055 in March 2009 and reached about 38,916, its old peak, 15 years later in early 2024. What compound annual growth rate did the index need over those 15 years? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Growth multiple = 38,916 ÷ 7,055 ≈ 5.52. Annual growth = 5.52 to the power 1/15, minus 1, ≈ 12.1% a year. Even a strong 15-year run of about 12% a year only brought the index back to where it had been in 1989. Buying near the peak cost Japanese investors a generation of returns.

children.text: Why the Cycle Would Not Turn

markDefs.definition: A downturn in which companies and households focus on paying down debt rather than borrowing and spending, even when interest rates are near zero, because their assets are worth less than their liabilities. The term was popularised by economist Richard Koo to describe Japan.
Companies that cannot earn enough to cover their debts but are kept alive by banks continuing to lend to them, often to avoid the bank recognising a loss.

children.text: Recall the Schumpeter idea from Lesson 1.2: cycles overlap, and the worst periods come when several engines point down together. In Japan almost all of them did. Two terms explain most of it. The first is a

cells: Banks avoided recognising bad loans for most of the 1990s, rolling over credit to zombie companies instead. Money that could have gone to healthy new businesses stayed trapped in failing ones
Companies whose land and shares had collapsed spent years repaying loans, so even near-zero interest rates failed to revive borrowing and investment
Prices drifted down for long stretches from the late 1990s. Consumers delayed purchases, and the real burden of debt rose, just as in the 1930s
Interest rates were cut too slowly at first, fiscal stimulus was stop-start, and a sales tax increase in 1997 hit a fragile recovery. Bold monetary easing came only much later
Japan's working-age population peaked in the mid 1990s and has shrunk since, reducing long-term demand for housing, credit and consumer goods. This is a Kuznets-style engine running in reverse

events.title: The banking crisis finally breaks
events.description: Hokkaido Takushoku Bank and Yamaichi Securities collapse in November 1997. The Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan and Nippon Credit Bank are nationalised in 1998. Bad loans can no longer be hidden.

events.title: Zero rates and the first QE
events.description: The Bank of Japan adopts a zero interest rate policy in 1999 and, in 2001, becomes the first major central bank to use quantitative easing, buying assets to push money into the system.

events.title: Forced clean-up
events.description: Regulators push the big banks to write off bad loans, and the banking system consolidates into a few large groups.

events.title: Abenomics
events.description: Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's government and the Bank of Japan under Haruhiko Kuroda launch aggressive monetary easing, fiscal support and structural reform. The yen weakens and the Nikkei begins a sustained recovery.

events.title: Governance reform
events.description: Japan introduces a Stewardship Code in 2014 and a Corporate Governance Code in 2015. In 2023 the Tokyo Stock Exchange presses companies trading below book value to improve returns for shareholders. Foreign investors, including Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, build large positions.

events.title: The cycle finally turns
events.description: The Nikkei closes above its 1989 peak in February 2024. In March the Bank of Japan raises rates for the first time in 17 years, ending its negative interest rate policy.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Why did Japanese banks' decision to keep lending to zombie companies make the downturn last longer, even though it avoided immediate bankruptcies?
options: It caused inflation to rise sharply
It kept capital and workers trapped in failing firms, while banks had less to lend to healthy and new businesses
It made the yen too weak for exporters
It forced the stock market to close
body.explanation: Evergreening bad loans avoided painful write-offs in the short term, but it kept unproductive firms alive, held down prices and wages in their industries, and tied up bank capital that healthy firms needed. The economy could not clear out the excesses of the boom, so the cycle could not complete its repair phase.

points: Recognition was also delayed for years, but the RBI's 2015 Asset Quality Review forced banks to disclose bad loans
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code of 2016 created a route to resolve failed companies

Positive inflation, a young population and rising incomes helped the economy grow out of the problem

body.text: Japan-style traps happen inside markets too, not just to whole countries. In India, the Nifty PSU Bank index spent most of the decade after 2010 far below its peak while bad loans built up, and the Nifty Realty index took well over a decade after 2008 to recover meaningfully. A sector or stock can stay in its own lost decade while the Nifty 50 makes new highs. Buying something only because it has fallen a long way, without asking whether its engines are repaired, is how investors get stuck.

body.title: Is This a Normal Downturn or a Japan-Style Trap?
steps: Were prices at extreme valuations at the peak, far above historical norms?
Was the boom funded by heavy borrowing against the same assets that are now falling?
Are lenders recognising and resolving bad loans, or quietly rolling them over?
Is inflation positive, helping debts shrink in real terms, or is there deflation?
Is the population or customer base still growing, or shrinking?
Is policy responding decisively, or slowly and reluctantly?
Is a new rally backed by repaired balance sheets and earnings, or only by hope?

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Companies that cannot service their debts but are kept alive because banks keep rolling over their loans are known as ___ companies.
body.explanation: Zombie companies were a central feature of Japan's lost decades. Economists Ricardo Caballero, Takeo Hoshi and Anil Kashyap showed how zombie lending depressed investment and productivity in the industries where it was common.

body.title: "Could India Become Japan?"
body.scenario: A colleague in your Mumbai office reads an article comparing Indian market valuations to Japan in 1989. He tells you: "The Nifty is expensive compared with other markets. Japan proves an index can go nowhere for 34 years. I'm moving my entire SIP portfolio into fixed deposits."
body.prompt: Using the checklist in this lesson, how would you evaluate his comparison? What is fair about his worry, and what is missing?
body.modelAnswer: His worry has a fair core. Starting valuation matters a great deal, as Japan in 1989 and the US in 1966 and 2000 all showed, and no index is guaranteed to recover quickly. But a single similarity is not enough. Japan's bust came from a combination: a market P/E of around 60 or more, a bubble funded by borrowing against land and shares, cross-shareholdings that tied banks and companies together, banks hiding bad loans for years, deflation, a shrinking workforce and slow policy. He should check how many of those conditions apply. India's valuations have at times been high relative to other markets, but Indian banks went through their bad loan clean-up after 2015, inflation is positive, the population is young and credit is not collapsing. That makes a full Japan-style repeat less likely, though valuations can still compress and returns can disappoint for years. Moving everything into fixed deposits also swaps one risk for another: inflation can erode FD returns after tax, as Lesson 2.3 showed. More balanced responses include continuing SIPs so he buys at many valuations rather than betting on one, keeping an asset allocation that matches his goals, and considering some diversification across asset classes and geographies so no single country's lost decade can sink his plan.

cards.definition: The 1985 agreement among major economies to weaken the US dollar. The resulting strong yen led Japan to cut rates, fuelling its bubble.
The 1980s practice of Japanese companies using borrowed money to speculate in financial markets alongside their core business.
Banks and companies owning stakes in each other. In Japan they spread the damage of falling share prices through the whole system.
A downturn in which borrowers focus on repaying debt rather than spending, so low interest rates fail to revive the economy.
A company unable to cover its debts that survives because banks keep rolling over its loans.
A strong rally inside a long bear market that convinces investors the bottom is in, before prices fall to new lows.

children.text: That completes the global tour: speculative manias, the Depression and the post-war boom, inflation and disinflation, and a cycle that refused to turn. Chapter 3 brings the same lens home, starting with India's markets before 1991, from brokers trading under a banyan tree in Bombay to the birth of the Sensex.

Comparisons with India are for education only, are not a forecast, and are not investment advice. Consult a SEBI registered investment adviser before changing your investments.

points: After the 1985 Plaza Accord, record-low Japanese interest rates fuelled a land and share bubble, and the Nikkei roughly tripled to 38,916 by December 1989
Rate hikes from 2.5% to 6% and limits on property lending reversed the credit loop, and the Nikkei fell almost 40% in 1990 alone
Three rallies of about 59%, 61% and 141% all proved to be false dawns, and the index was about 82% below its peak in March 2009
Hidden bad loans, zombie companies, a balance sheet recession, deflation, slow policy and a shrinking workforce kept the cycle from turning
The Nikkei took 34 years to regain its 1989 peak, finally doing so in February 2024 after bank clean-ups, Abenomics and governance reform
India faced its own bad loan cycle after 2015 but forced recognition, created the IBC and grew out of it with positive inflation and a young population
Lost decades can hit sectors and single stocks even when the broad index is rising, so check whether the engines are repaired before assuming a recovery
